title: Monitor the operation and maintenance of irrigation systems

lessons.title: Irrigation scheduling
lessons.html:
How much water, and when?

An irrigation schedule tells the team when to irrigate each block and how much water to apply. A good schedule gives the crop what it needs, no more and no less. Too little water lowers yield and quality; too much wastes water and electricity, leaches fertiliser, waterlogs roots and encourages disease.

Information needed for a schedule

  • Crop and growth stage: young plants use little water; water use peaks during flowering and fruit or grain fill.
  • Weather: hot, dry and windy days increase crop water use. Rain reduces the need to irrigate.
  • Soil: sandy soils hold little water and need short, frequent irrigations; clay soils hold more and need longer intervals.
  • Root depth: water only the root zone; water below it is lost.
  • System delivery rate: how many millimetres per hour the system applies.

Methods

  • Soil moisture monitoring: probes, tensiometers or the feel method tell you when the soil is getting dry.
  • Weather-based: evaporation data from a weather station or service gives estimated crop water use.
  • Adviser schedules: irrigation consultants or software provide schedules for each block.

Modifying the schedule

A schedule is a starting point, not a fixed rule. If 25 mm of rain fell overnight, postpone irrigation on blocks that received it and check soil moisture before restarting. In a heat wave, the interval may need to shorten. Record every change and the reason.

Example

A drip system delivers 2 mm per hour and the block needs 10 mm. Run time is 10 divided by 2, which is 5 hours.

lessons.title: Efficient operation and data recording
lessons.html:
Running the system well

Daily checks during irrigation

  • Pressure at the pump, at the filter (before and after) and at the end of the line. A big pressure difference across the filter means it is blocked.
  • Flow meter reading at start and end.
  • Leaks, burst pipes and broken sprinklers.
  • Blocked drippers or sprinklers that do not turn.
  • Wet spots and dry spots in the land.
  • Centre pivots: check tower alignment, wheel tracks and end guns.

Efficiency tips

  • Irrigate in the cooler parts of the day or at night where possible to reduce evaporation, and use off-peak electricity tariffs where available.
  • Do not irrigate in strong wind with sprinklers.
  • Fix leaks immediately.
  • Keep the system's pressure in the range the designer specified.

Data to collect

DataWhy
Date, block, start and end timeShows what was applied
Meter readings (m³)Water use and compliance with the water use authorisation
PressuresEarly warning of blockages or leaks
RainfallAdjusting the schedule
Soil moisture readingsChecking whether the schedule is right
Faults and repairsMaintenance planning

Water use from rivers, dams and boreholes may need registration or a licence under the National Water Act 36 of 1998. Accurate meter records protect the farm.

Review the data weekly with the irrigation team. Compare water applied with the schedule and soil moisture readings, and look for blocks that always need more water; they may have leaks, blocked drippers or poor pressure.

Keep the records in one file per block so they can be compared from season to season.

lessons.title: Maintenance programmes and supervising teams
lessons.html:
Planned maintenance

A maintenance programme lists each part of the system, what must be done, how often and by whom. Planned maintenance prevents breakdowns in the hottest, busiest weeks.

FrequencyTasks
Daily (when running)Check pressures, leaks, filters, pump noise and heat
WeeklyClean or backflush filters, flush ends of drip lines, check sprinklers
MonthlyCheck valves, pressure regulators, meter accuracy, pivot gearboxes and tyres
Each seasonAcid or chlorine treatment of drip lines as advised, pump service, replace worn nozzles, test system uniformity

Keep a stock of common spares (couplings, drippers, nozzles, clamps) and record all repairs with date and cost.

Supervising irrigation activities

  • Give each irrigator a written daily plan: blocks, times, valves to open and close.
  • Train workers on the system, the checks to do and how to record readings.
  • Check their records daily and walk the blocks to confirm.
  • Make sure faults are reported and fixed, and give feedback.

Safety

  • Only qualified, authorised people work on pump electrics and control panels. Lock out and tag out power before working on pumps.
  • Chemicals for cleaning drip lines (acids, chlorine) and fertigation products need PPE: gloves, goggles, apron. Always add acid to water, never water to acid.
  • Prevent backflow of fertiliser or chemicals into boreholes and rivers with the correct valves.
  • Keep clear of moving pivots and reels.

Key points

  • Base schedules on crop stage, soil, weather and system delivery rate, and adjust after rain or heat.
  • Run time equals water needed divided by the system's delivery rate.
  • Check pressures, filters and leaks every time the system runs.
  • Record meter readings, rainfall, soil moisture and faults.
  • Plan maintenance and supervise teams with written daily plans and safety rules.
